entries.2565908b62295802a5bfacf5b8472c972ce97741: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.9.6" sID="gen122268" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6.</hi> <hi type="italic">Now the case is this</hi> <note n="719"> <div sID="gen122270" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Or ie di ceci</foreign>;” — “Now this I say.”<div eID="gen122270" type="x-p"/> </note> He now commends alms-giving by a beautiful similitude, comparing it to sowing. For in sowing, the seed is cast forth by the hand, is scattered upon the ground on this side and on that, is harrowed, and at length rots; and thus it seems as good as lost. The case is similar as to alms-giving. What goes from you to some other quarter seems as if it were, diminishing of what you have, but the season of harvest will come, when the fruit will be gathered. For as the Lord reckons every thing that is laid out upon the poor as given to himself, so he afterwards requites it with large interest. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Prov.19.17">Proverbs 19:17</reference>.)<div eID="gen122269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122271" type="x-p"/>Now for Paul’s similitude. He that<hi type="italic"> sows sparingly</hi> will have a poor harvest, corresponding to the sowing: he that <hi type="italic">sows bountifully</hi> and with a full hand, will reap a correspondingly bountiful harvest. Let this doctrine be deeply rooted in our minds, that, whenever carnal reason keeps us back from doing good through fear of loss, we may immediately defend ourselves with this shield — “But the Lord declares that we are <hi type="italic">sowing.</hi>” The <hi type="italic">harvest, </hi>however, should be explained as referring to the spiritual recompense of eternal life, as well as to earthly blessings, which God confers upon the beneficent. For God requites, not only in heaven, but also in this world, the beneficence of believers. Hence it is as though he had said, “The more beneficent you are to your neighbors, you will find the blessing of God so much the more abundantly poured out upon you.” He again contrasts here <hi type="italic">blessing </hi>with <hi type="italic">sparing, </hi>as he had previously done with <hi type="italic">niggardliness. </hi>Hence it appears, that it is taken to mean — a large and bountiful liberality.<div eID="gen122271" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122268" osisID="2Cor.9.6" type="section"/>
entries.dbabf7222f6e98191d2457c106dc7206a3bd2ebe: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.9.7" sID="gen122272" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122273" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7</hi> <hi type="italic"> Every one according to the purpose of his heart.</hi> As he had enjoined it upon them to give liberally, this, also, required to be added — that liberality is estimated by God, not so much from the sum, as from the disposition. He was desirous, it is true, to induce them to give largely, in order that the brethren might be the more abundantly aided; but he had no wish to extort any thing from them against their will. Hence he exhorts them to give willingly, whatever they might be prepared to give. He places <hi type="italic">purpose of heart</hi> in contrast with <hi type="italic">regret </hi>and <hi type="italic">constraint. </hi>For what we do, when compelled by necessity, is not done by us with <hi type="italic">purpose of heart,</hi> but with reluctance. <note n="720"> <div sID="gen122274" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">Auec </hi>regret et tristesse</foreign>;” — “With regret and sadness.”<div eID="gen122274" type="x-p"/> </note> Now the <hi type="italic">necessity</hi> meant you must understand to be what is extrinsic, as it is called — that is, what springs from the influence of others. For we obey God, because it is <hi type="italic">necessary,</hi> and yet we do it willingly. We ourselves, accordingly, in that case impose a necessity of our own accord, and because the flesh is reluctant, we often even constrain ourselves to perform a duty that is necessary for us. But, when we are constrained from the influence of others, having in the mean time an inclination to avoid it, if by any means we could, we do nothing in that case with alacrity — nothing with cheerfulness, but every thing with reluctance or constraint of mind.<div eID="gen122273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122275" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For God loveth a cheerful giver</hi> He calls us back to God, as I said in the outset, for alms are a sacrifice. Now no sacrifice is pleasing to God, if it is not voluntary. For when he teaches us, that <hi type="italic">God loveth a cheerful giver, </hi>he intimates that, on the other hand, the niggardly and reluctant are loathed by Him. For He does not wish to lord it over us, in the manner of a tyrant, but, as He acts towards us as a Father, so he requires from us the cheerful obedience of children. <note n="721"> <div sID="gen122276" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vne obeissance filiale, qui soit prompte et franche</foreign>;” — “A filial obedience, which is prompt and cheerful.”<div eID="gen122276" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen122275" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122272" osisID="2Cor.9.7" type="section"/>
entries.99f0bed56973639682270c7e301cda69ff37834e: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.9.8" sID="gen122277" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122278" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi> <hi type="italic">And God is able</hi> Again he provides against the base thought, which our infidelity constantly suggests to us. “What! will you not rather have a regard to your own interest? Do you not consider, that when this is taken away, there will be so much the less left for yourself?” With the view of driving away this, Paul arms us with a choice promise — that whatever we give away will turn out to our advantage. I have said already, that we are by nature excessively niggardly — because we are prone to distrust, which tempts every one to retain with eager grasp what belongs to him. For correcting this fault, we must lay hold of this promise — that those that do good to the poor do no less provide for their own interests than if they were watering their lands. For by alms-givings, like so many canals, they make the blessing of God flow forth towards themselves, so as to be enriched by it. What Paul means is this: “Such liberality will deprive you of nothing, but God will make it return to you in much greater abundance.” For he speaks of the power of God, not as the Poets do, but after the manner of Scripture, which ascribes to him a power put forth in action, the present efficacy of which we ourselves feel — not any inactive power that we merely imagine.<div eID="gen122278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122279" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That having all sufficiency in all things</hi> He mentions a twofold advantage arising from that grace, which he had promised to the Corinthians — that they should have what is enough for themselves, and would have something over and above for doing good. By the term <hi type="italic">sufficiency</hi> he points out the measure which the Lord knows to be useful for us, for it is not always profitable for us, to be filled to satiety. The Lord therefore, ministers to us according to the measure of our advantage, sometimes more, sometimes less, but in such a way that we are satisfied — which is much more, than if one had the whole world to luxuriate upon. In this <hi type="italic">sufficiency</hi> we must abound, for the purpose of doing good to others, for the reason why God does us good is — not that every one may keep to himself what he has received, but that there may be a mutual participation among us, according as necessity may require.<div eID="gen122279" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122277" osisID="2Cor.9.8" type="section"/>

9. As it is written, He hath dispersed He brings forward a proof from Psalms 112:9, where, along with other excellencies of the pious man, the Prophet mentions this, too, — that he will not be wanting in doing good, but as water flows forth incessantly from a perennial fountain, so the gushing forth of his liberality will be unceasing. Paul has an eye to this — that we be not weary in well doing, (Galatians 6:9,) and this is also what the Prophet’s words mean.
“Our author, when commenting on the passage here referred to, remarks: “This passage is quoted by Paul, (2 Corinthians 9:9,) in which he informs us, that it is an easy matter for God to bless us with plenty, so that we may exercise our bounty freely, deliberately, and impartially, and this accords best with the design of the Prophet.” — Calvin on the Psalms, vol. 4, p. 329. — Ed.

entries.a2510f22a73703a3034d90b1d5b39daf7a6e10f0: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.9.10" sID="gen122299" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122300" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi> <hi type="italic">He that supplieth.</hi> A beautieth circumlocution, in place of the term <hi type="italic">God, </hi>and full of consolation. <note n="724"> <div sID="gen122301" type="x-p"/> “The words <foreign xml:lang="el">ὁ ἐπιχορηγῶν βρῶσιν </foreign>are a periphrasis of God (<hi type="italic">i.e., </hi>the <hi type="italic">Good Being</hi>) ‘who giveth us all things richly to enjoy.’ It is formed on <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.55.10">Isaiah 55:10</reference>.” — Bloomfield. — Ed.<div eID="gen122301" type="x-p"/> </note> For the person that sows seed in the proper season, appears when reaping to gather the fruit of his labor and industry, and sowing appears as though it were the fountainhead from which food flows forth to us. Paul opposes this idea, by maintaining that the seed is afforded and the food is furnished by the favor of God even to the husbandmen that sow, and who are looked upon as supporting themselves and others by their efforts. There is a similar statement in <reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.8.16 Bible:Deut.8.18">Deuteronomy 8:16,18</reference> —<div eID="gen122300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122302" type="x-p"/>God fed thee with manna — food which thy fathers knew not: lest perhaps when thou hast come into the land which he shall give thee, thou shouldst say, My hand and my strength have gotten, me this wealth; for it is the Lord that giveth power to get wealth, etc.<div eID="gen122302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122303" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Supply</hi> Here there are two different readings, even in the Greek versions. For some manuscripts render the three verbs in the future — <hi type="italic">will supply, will multiply, will increase.</hi> <note n="725"> <div sID="gen122304" type="x-p"/> “The Vatican MS. reads with the futures — <foreign xml:lang="el">χορηγήσει </foreign>(<hi type="italic">will supply,</hi>)<foreign xml:lang="el"> πληθύνεῖ,</foreign> (<hi type="italic">will supply,</hi>) and <foreign xml:lang="el">αὐξήσει,</foreign> (<hi type="italic">will increase</hi>) ” — <hi type="italic">Penn.</hi> — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen122304" type="x-p"/> </note> In this way, there would be a confirmation of the foregoing statement, for it is no rare thing with Paul to repeat the same promise in different words, that it may be the better impressed upon men’s minds. In other manuscripts these words occur in the infinitive mood, and it is well known that the infinitive is sometimes used in place of the optative. I rather prefer this reading, both because it is the more generally received one, and because Paul is accustomed to follow up his exhortations with prayers, entreating from God what he had previously comprised in his doctrine; though at the same time the former reading would not be unsuitable.<div eID="gen122303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122305" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Bread for food</hi> He mentions a two-fold fruit of the blessing of God upon us — <hi type="italic">first</hi>, that we have sufficiency for ourselves for the support of life; and, <hi type="italic">secondly, </hi>that we have something to lay up for relieving the necessities of others. For as we are not born for ourselves merely, <note n="726"> <div sID="gen122306" type="x-p"/> Our Author has here very probably in his eye a celebrated passage in Horace — “<foreign xml:lang="la">Nos numerus sumus, et fruges consumere nati</foreign>;” — “We do but add to the numbers of mankind, and seem born only to consume the fruits of the earth.” (Hot. <reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.1.2 Bible:Eph.1.27">Ep. 1:2, 27</reference>.) — Ed.<div eID="gen122306" type="x-p"/> </note> so a Christian man ought neither to live to himself, nor lay out what he has, merely for his own use.<div eID="gen122305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122307" type="x-p"/>Under the terms <hi type="italic">seed, </hi>and <hi type="italic">fruits of righteousness, </hi>he refers to <hi type="italic">alms. </hi>The <hi type="italic">fruits of righteousness</hi> he indirectly contrasts with those returns that the greater number lay up in cellars, barns, and keeping-places, that they may, every one of them, cram in whatever they can gather, nay, scrape together, so as to enrich themselves. By the former term he expresses the means of doing good; by the <hi type="italic">latter </hi>the work itself, or office of love; <note n="727"> <div sID="gen122308" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">L’assistance laquelle on fait par charite</foreign>;” — “The assistance which one gives in love.”<div eID="gen122308" type="x-p"/> </note> for <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> is taken here, by <hi type="italic">synecdoche, </hi>to mean <hi type="italic">beneficence. </hi>“May God not only supply you with what may be sufficient for every one’s private use, but also to such an extent, that the fountain of your liberality, ever flowing forth, may never be exhausted!” If, however, it is one department of <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> — as assuredly it is not the least <note n="728"> <div sID="gen122309" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Comme a la verite s’en est vne des prineipales</foreign>;” — “As in truth it is one of the chief’.”<div eID="gen122309" type="x-p"/> </note> — to relieve the necessities of neighbors, those must be unrighteous who neglect this department of duty.<div eID="gen122307" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122299" osisID="2Cor.9.10" type="section"/>
entries.7097fc206ca0f464fd9582fb5e526160ac0f67e9: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.9.11" sID="gen122310" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122311" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11.</hi> <hi type="italic">May be enriched unto all bountifulness.</hi> Again he makes use of the term <hi type="italic">bountifulness,</hi> to express the nature of true liberality — when,<div eID="gen122311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122312" type="x-p"/>casting all our care upon God, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.5.7">1 Peter 5:7</reference>,)<div eID="gen122312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122313" type="x-p"/>we cheerfully lay out what belongs to us for whatever purposes He directs. He teaches us <note n="729"> <div sID="gen122314" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Or yci il nous remonstre et donne a entendre</foreign>;” — “Now here he shows us and gives us to understand.”<div eID="gen122314" type="x-p"/> </note> that these are the true riches of believers, when, relying upon the providence of God for the sufficiency of their support, they are not by distrust kept back from doing good. Nor is it without good reason, that he dignifies with the title of affluence the satisfying abundance of a mind that is simple, and contented with its moderate share; for nothing is more famished and starved than the distrustful, who are tormented with an anxious desire of having.<div eID="gen122313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122315" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Which produces through you.</hi> He commends, in consideration of another result, the alms which they were about to bestow — that they would tend to promote the glory of God. He afterwards, too, expresses this more distinctly, with amplification, in this way: “Besides the ordinary advantage of love, they will also produce thanksgiving.” Now he amplifies by saying, that <hi type="italic">thanks will be given to God by many,</hi> and that, not merely for the liberality itself, by which they have been helped, but also for the entire measure of piety among the Corinthians.<div eID="gen122315" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122310" osisID="2Cor.9.11" type="section"/>
entries.2690616b05329b0477fca2c75f6af54129c95325: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.9.12" sID="gen122316" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122317" type="x-p"/>By the term <hi type="italic">administration, </hi>he means what he had undertaken at the request of the Churches. Now what we render <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">functionem</hi></foreign> (<hi type="italic">service</hi>)<hi type="italic">, </hi>is in the Greek <foreign xml:lang="el">λειτουργία </foreign>term that sometimes denotes a sacrifice, sometimes any office that is publicly assigned. <note n="730"> <div sID="gen122318" type="x-p"/> The term <foreign xml:lang="el">λειτουργία </foreign>is very frequently made use of in the Septuagint, in connection with the sacrifices and other services of the priests and Levites. (See <reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.38.21">Exodus 38:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Num.4.24">Numbers 4:24</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Bible:Num.8.22">Numbers 8:22</reference>.) It is commonly employed by the Greek writers to denote a public service, more especially at Athens, discharged by the richer citizens at their own expense, and usually in rotation. The <foreign xml:lang="el">λειτουργοὶ,</foreign> says <hi type="italic">Potter, </hi>in his Grecian Antiquities, (volume 1,) were “persons of considerable estates, who, by their own tribe, or the whole people, were ordered to perform some public duty, or supply the commonwealth with necessaries at their own expenses. Of these there were diverse sorts, all of which were elected out of twelve hundred of the richest citizens, who were appointed by the people to undergo, when they should be required, all the burdensome and chargeable offices in the commonwealth, every tribe electing an hundred and twenty out of their own body, though this was contrary to Solon’s constitution, by which every man, of what quality soever, was obliged to serve the public according to his ability, with this exception only, that two offices should not be imposed on the same person at once, as we are informed by Demosthenes, in his oration against Leptines, where he likewise mentions an ancient law, requiring every man to undergo some <foreign xml:lang="el">λειτουργία </foreign>every second year.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen122318" type="x-p"/> </note> Either of them will suit this passage well. For on the one hand, it is no unusual thing for alms to be termed sacrifices; and, on the other hand, as on occasion of offices being distributed among citizens, <note n="731"> <div sID="gen122319" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Les charges estans distribuees, en vne ville entre les citoyens d’icelle</foreign>;” — “Offices being distributed in a town among the citizens of it.”<div eID="gen122319" type="x-p"/> </note> no one grudges to undertake the duty that has been assigned him, so in the Church, imparting to others ought to be looked upon as a necessary duty. <note n="732"> <div sID="gen122320" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ainsi en l’Eglise la communication consiste en ce que chacun s’acquitte enuers ses prochains de ce qu’il leur doit en charite</foreign>;” — “So in the Church, imparting to others consists in every one’s discharging to his neighbours, what he owes them, in love.”<div eID="gen122320" type="x-p"/> </note> The Corinthians, therefore, and others, by assisting the brethren at Jerusalem, presented a sacrifice to God, or they discharged a service that was proper, and one which they were bound to fulfill. Paul was the minister of that sacrifice, but the term <hi type="italic">ministry, </hi>or <hi type="italic">service, </hi>may also be viewed as referring to the Corinthians. It is, however, of no particular importance.<div eID="gen122317" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122316" osisID="2Cor.9.12" type="section"/>
entries.9982294c2f2ecf391a6f54d3fbe519cb8bc48758: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.9.13" sID="gen122321" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122322" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13. </hi><hi type="italic">By the experiment of that administration</hi> The term <hi type="italic">experiment</hi> here, as in a variety of other places, means <hi type="italic">proof </hi>or <hi type="italic">trial</hi> <note n="733"> <div sID="gen122323" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Tesmoignage, enseignement, ou experience</foreign>;” — “Proof, voucher, or trial.”<div eID="gen122323" type="x-p"/> </note> For it was a sufficient token for bringing the love of the Corinthians to the test, — that they were so liberal to brethren that were at a great distance from them. Paul, however, extends it farther — to their concurrent obedience in the gospel. <note n="734"> <div sID="gen122324" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Leur obeissance qu’ils rendoyent tons d’vn accord a l’euangile</foreign>;” — “Their obedience which they rendered, all with one accord, to the gospel.”<div eID="gen122324" type="x-p"/> </note> For by such proofs we truly manifest, that we are obedient to the doctrine of the gospel. Now their concurrence appears from this — that alms are conferred with the common consent of all.<div eID="gen122322" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.9.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122321" osisID="2Cor.9.13" type="section"/>

14. And their prayer He omits no advantage which may be of any use for stirring up the Corinthians.
“Qui puisse seruir a esmouuoir et encourager les Corinthtens.” — “That may serve to stir up and encourage the Corinthians.”
In the first place, he has made mention of the comfort that believers would experience; secondly, the thanksgiving, by means of which God was to be glorified. Nay more, he has said that this would be a confession, which would manifest to all their unanimous concurrence in faith, and in pious obedience. He now adds the reward that the Corinthians would receive from the saints — good-will springing from gratitude,
“Procedante de la recognoissance du benefice qu’ils auoyent receu des Corinthtens;” — “Proceeding from an acknowledgment of the kindness that they had received from the Corinthians.”
and earnest prayers. “They will have,” says he, “the means of requiting you in return; for they will regard you with the love with which they ought, and they will be careful to commend you to God in their prayers.” At length, as though he had obtained his desire, he prepares himself
“D’vne grande affection;” — “With great ardour.”
to celebrate the praises of God, by which he was desirous to testify the confidence felt by him, as though the matter were already accomplished.
CHAPTER 10
2 Corinthians 10:1-6
1. Now I Paul myself beseech you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, who in presence am base among you, but being absent am bold toward you:
1. Pro ipse ego Paulus exhortor vos
“Je vous exhorte, ou prie;” — “I exhort or entreat you.”
per lenitatem et mansuetudinem Christi, qui secundum faciem humilis quidem sum inter vos, absens autem audax sum in vos.
2. But I beseech you, that I may not be bold when I am present with that confidence, wherewith I think to be bold against some, which think of us as if we walked according to the flesh.
2. Rogo autem, ne praesens audeam ea fiducia, qua cogito audax esse in quosdam, qui nos aestimant, acsi secundum carnem ambularemus.
3. For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh:
3. Nam in carne ambulantes, non secundum carnem militamus.
4. (For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
4. Siquidem arma militiae nostrae non carnilia sunt, sed potentia Deo ad destructionem munitionum, quibus consilia destruimus.
5. Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;
5. Et omnem celsitudinem, quae extollitur adversus cognitionem Dei: et captivam ducimus omnem cogitationem ad obediendum Christo:
“Et reduisons en captiuite toute intelligence, ou, amenans conme prisonnier, toute,” etc.; — “And we bring into captivity every thought, or, leading forth as a prisoner every,” etc.
6. And having in a readiness to revenge all disobedience, when your obedience is fulfilled.
6. Et in promptu habemus vindictam adversus omnem inobedientiam, quum impleta fuerit vestra obedientia.

               <ns0:head>CHAP. IX.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 FOr as touching <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 8.4.</ns0:note> the ministring to the Saints, it is superfluous for me to write unto you <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">I should think the Particle <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, here translated <ns0:hi>for,</ns0:hi> had been better translated <ns0:hi>But,</ns0:hi> as in 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 4.15. 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.9. our Translators do render it. So these words contain an elegant revocation of himself from the Argument he had dwelt upon in the whole former Chapter, and the sense amounts to this: But to what purpose do I multiply words to you, to perswade you to minister to the Saints in distress? as to you it is superfluous. By this Art letting them know, that he had, no doubt, but a confident expectation concerning them; the suggesting of which hath also the force of another Argument, that they might not deceive the Apostles good opinion and confidence of them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 For I know the forwardness of your mind, for which I boast of you to them of Macedonia, that Achaia was ready a year ago <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He gives them the reason why he judgeth it superfluous to write to them, because they had a forward mind of themselves, and needed not to be spurred on. This the Apostle tells them that <ns0:hi>he knew,</ns0:hi> (he had told them of it, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 8.10.) he knew it either from themselves, or from some that came from them unto him; and he had boasted of them for this their forwardness in this good work to the Churches of <ns0:hi>Macedonia.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and your zeal hath provoked very many <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">He tells them, that their warmth unto, and in, this work, had kindled an heat in many in those parts where he was. Having therefore been so forward in this good work, and so good instruments to kindle an heat in others, he would not have them now come behind others, or grow cold in it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Yet have I sent the brethren, lest our boasting of you should be in vain in this behalf <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">I did not send the Brethren so much to move you to this work, or quicken you to it, for you your selves purposed it a year ago, and shewed a forwardness in it; the motion proceed<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed from your selves, and you shewed a readiness to it, which gave me occasion to boast of you to the Churches of <ns0:hi>Macedonia:</ns0:hi> but I thought you might forget it, and I would not have our boast<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing in vain on this behalf.</ns0:note>, that, as I said, ye may be ready <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">And besides, I would have the work done, that your Alms might not be to gather when I come, (as he had said 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 16.2.) but might be in a readiness to be taken and carried away, (for that is signified here by be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing ready) not that readiness of mind of which he had before spoken, and which he had before mentioned as what he had found in them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:468" />4 Lest haply, if they of Macedonia come with me, and find you unprepared, we (that we say not you) should be ashamed in this same confident boasting <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">For if I should come, and any of the Members of the Chur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ches of <ns0:hi>Macedonia,</ns0:hi> who have heard me boasting of you as a people very forward in this charitable work, and when they are come, they should find you had done nothing, only talked much of your readiness; both I should be ashamed, and you also might see some cause to blush, which I, who consult your honour and reputation equally with my own, would prevent.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Therefore I thought it necessary to exhort the brethren, that they would go before unto you, and make up before hand <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>blessing.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> your bounty, <ns0:note n="|" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>which had <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> spoken of <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> whereof ye had notice before <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This was the cause why I judged it reasonable to send the three Brethren, before mentioned, unto you, that they might make up your bounty; <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, not so much to move, quick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />en, or exhort you to it, as to hasten the dispatch, and perfecting of it, that your money might be ready gathered. The word which we translate Bounty, in the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> signifieth <ns0:hi>Blessing,</ns0:hi> which a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />greeth with the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Dialect. <ns0:hi>Abigails</ns0:hi> Present to <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> in his distress is called <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, a Blessing, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 25.27. so <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> called his Present to his Brother <ns0:hi>Esau, Gen.</ns0:hi> 33.11. Such kind of reliefs are called a <ns0:hi>Blessing</ns0:hi> in both the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> Tongue: 1. Because they are a part of Gods blessing upon him that gives, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 24.5. 2. Because the giving of them is a re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cognition or acknowledgment how far God hath blessed persons, they giving as the Lord hath prospered them, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 16.2. 3. Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they are an indication of the blessing, or well wishing of him that giveth to him that receiveth the gift. 4. Because they are a real doing good to the person that receiveth them, an a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctual blessing of him. 5. Possibly they are (in him that gives) an effectual, real blessing of God; for we then bless God with what we have, when we use and improve it for the ends for which he hath given it to us. It is very observable, That a li<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />beral free giving to the relief of the Servants of God in distress, is called <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> and <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>Grace</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Blessing.</ns0:hi> An heart to it being created in us from the free Grace of God, and the work it self being a real, actual blessing of God with our substance, and the fruit of our increase: which two things well digested, will be potent Arguments to Charity with every Soul that knoweth any thing of God, or hath any Love for God.</ns0:note>, that the same might be ready <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">That the same may be ready gathered <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> not to gather when I come.</ns0:note> as a <ns0:hi>matter of</ns0:hi> bounty <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">As a Blessing, we translate it <ns0:hi>as a matter of bounty:</ns0:hi> the sense is the same.</ns0:note>, and not as of covetousness <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Not of <ns0:hi>Covetousness:</ns0:hi> The meaning is, I have also sent the Brethren, that they may perswade you to a free and liberal Contribution, a giving that may look like a <ns0:hi>Blessing,</ns0:hi> not as pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceeding from a narrow heart, in which the love of money pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vaileth above the Love of God. Giving to the distressed Saints of God sparingly, and disproportionately to what Estate we have, no way looks like a Blessing; he that so gives, doth not, according to the Apostles Phrase, give <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> for he neither gives as the Lord hath blessed and prospered him, nor yet according to what God requires of him; for he withholds a part of what he ought to part with: neither doth he <ns0:hi>bless his Brother</ns0:hi>; he doth him some little good, but <ns0:hi>blessing another</ns0:hi> signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifies a more liberal doing good to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 But this <ns0:hi>I say,</ns0:hi>

                     </ns0:gap> 6.7, 9.</ns0:note> He which soweth sparingly, shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully, shall reap also bountifully <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Whereas covetous persons think all lost which they give to charitable uses, the Apostle correcteth their mistake, by letting them know, that it is no more lost, than the seed is which the Husbandman casteth into his ground, which bringeth forth thirty, sixty, or sometimes an hundred-<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>old; though with this difference, that whereas the Husbandmans Crop dependeth up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on the goodness and preparedness of his ground, it is not so with this spiritual Crop; a man shall not reap according to the nature of the Soil in which he casts his seed; for he that giveth to a Prophet, or to a righteous man, in the name of a Prophet, or a righteous man, (though he may be mistaken in the person to whom he so giveth) yet shall he receive the reward of a Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet, and of a righteous man: But this spiritual Sower shall re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive, according to the quantity of seed which he soweth. He that soweth niggardly and sparingly, shall reap accordingly; he which soweth liberally, shall reap liberally: From whence we may be confirmed, that the rewards of another life will not be equal, but bear some proportion to the good works which men have done here.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, <ns0:hi>so let him give,</ns0:hi>

                     </ns0:gap> 12.8.</ns0:note> not grudgingly, or of ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessity: for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 25.2. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 5.</ns0:note> God loveth a cheerful giver <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Let not any give out of any awe of us, nor as it were for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ced by our Authority, but as God shall put it into his heart, and as he hath purposed in himself, and is inclined from him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self, without any grudging, or unwillingness; not because he thinks he must give, but out of choice: for God loveth one that giveth with freedom and cheerfulness, not him that giveth as it were by constraint, or upon force; it is the <ns0:hi>Will</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Affic<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion</ns0:hi> of the Giver, not the quantity of the gift that God looks at. The Apostle, by naming God and his acceptance in the case, lets the <ns0:hi>Corinthians</ns0:hi> know, that God was concerned in what they thus gave; it was not given to men only: according to that, <ns0:hi>He that hath pity on the poor, lendeth to the Lord, and that which he hath given, will he pay him again,</ns0:hi> Prov. 19.17.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 And God <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> able to make all grace to abound towards you <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Having made God in the Verse before a Debtor to those, who by giving to poor distressed Saints, would make him their Creditor; he here proveth him to be no insolvent Debtor, but able to do much more for them, than they in this thing should do at his command out of love to him. He is (saith he) able to make <ns0:hi>all Grace to abound towards you</ns0:hi>; the word translated Grace, signifieth all sorts of gifts, whether of a temporal, or spiritual nature; and being here applied to God, (who is the Author of all gifts) it may very properly be interpreted concer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning both. God is able to repay you in temporal things what you thus lend him, and so to pay you <ns0:hi>in Specie</ns0:hi>; and he is able to pay you <ns0:hi>in Value,</ns0:hi> by spiritual habits and influences.</ns0:note>, that ye always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That you may have a sufficiency in all things, so as that you may abound to, and in every good work.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 As it is written, He hath dispersed abroad: he hath given to the poor: his righteousness re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />maineth for ever <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">As in the former Verse the Apostle had asserted Gods Suf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ficiency to repay them what they should lend him, so he here asserteth Gods readiness and willingness. This he confirmeth from a promise taken out of <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 112.9. (where also is further added—<ns0:hi>his horn shall be exalted with honour.</ns0:hi>) Concerning the merciful man, it is true that <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>There is that scat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tereth, and yet increaseth.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Psalmist</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>His righteousness remaineth for ever</ns0:hi>: by which term some understand his <ns0:hi>bounty</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>liberality:</ns0:hi> I had rather understand by it here his <ns0:hi>obedience</ns0:hi> to the Command of God in his free distribution to the poor: this remaineth in Gods Book of remembrance for ever, God will not forget this labour of love, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 6.10. The friends which he maketh with his <ns0:hi>Mammon of Vnrighteousness,</ns0:hi> shall <ns0:hi>re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive him into everlasting habitations.</ns0:hi> A mans riches cannot re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />main for ever, but his <ns0:hi>Righteousness,</ns0:hi> in the distribution of them, according to the Command of God, that shall remain for ever.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Now he that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 55.10.</ns0:note> ministreth seed to the sow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The God, whose Providence and Blessing maketh rich, and who giveth this seed to the sower,</ns0:note>, both minister bread for your food <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">supply you with whatso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ever you stand in need of for this life,</ns0:note>, and mul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiply your seed sown, and increase the fruits of your righteousness <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">and give you an heart to multiply that spiritual seed, by which the fruits of your Righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness shall be increased. Some <ns0:hi>Greek Copies</ns0:hi> read these words in the Future tense, according to which reading they are a formal promise, both of good things, whereby they might shew their Charity; and also of a free and large heart, disposing them to that exercise of Grace. Our Translators render it in the form of a Prayer; which yet being the Prayer of the Apostle, put up in Faith, doth virtually contain a promise both of a <ns0:hi>tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />poral,</ns0:hi> and a <ns0:hi>spiritual increase.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Being inriched in every thing to all bounti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fulness <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The word here translated <ns0:hi>Bountifulness,</ns0:hi> signifies <ns0:hi>Simplicity,</ns0:hi> in opposition to deceit and fraud. We had it before <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 8.2. so <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.8. so <ns0:hi>Iam.</ns0:hi> 1.5. God is said to give <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> simply, (we translate it <ns0:hi>liberally.</ns0:hi>) We have in these two Chapters met with three words, by which the bounty of Christians to persons in distress, is expressed; <ns0:hi>Grace, Blessing, Simplicity,</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. The first lets us know the true root of all acceptable giving to those who are in distress, that must be <ns0:hi>free Love:</ns0:hi> the second expresseth the true end, <ns0:hi>Blessing God</ns0:hi> and our Neighbour, serving the Glory and Commands of God, and the necessities of our Brethren: this third expresseth the manner how we must give, that is, with <ns0:hi>simplicity.</ns0:hi> It is no true libera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lity where <ns0:hi>simplicity</ns0:hi> is wanting; that a man doth not what he doth with a plain heart and design to obey God, and do good to his Brother.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 1.11. & 4.15.</ns0:note> which causeth through us thanksgiving to God <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">As a further Argument to press them to this liberality, he tells them, That it would cause them that were the Apostles and Ministers of Christ, to offer Thanksgiving unto God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 For the administration of this service not only supplieth the want of the saints, but is abun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dant also by many thanksgivings unto God <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">No man ought to live to himself. The two great ends of every Christians life ought to be the Glory of God, and the good of others, especially such as belong to the Houshold of Faith. This Service (saith the Apostle) serveth both those ends; 1. It supplieth the necessities of the Saints: and, 2. It causeth Thanksgivings to God by many persons, and upon ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny accounts, (which he further openeth in the following verses)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:469" />13 Whilst by the experiment of this ministrati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Upon their receiving of what you sent them,</ns0:note>, they glorifie God for your professed subje<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction unto the gospel of Christ <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">they will see how ready you are to obey the Gospel of Christ, (which hath in so many places called you to this duty) and this will give them occasion of blessing God, who in the day of his pow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er, hath made such a willing people, willing at Gods command and in consideration of the Love of Christ, to strip themselves to cloath his naked Members, to restrain their own appetites to feed them. The Grace of God bestowed on others, is mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter of great thanksgiving to every gracious heart.</ns0:note>, and for your li<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />beral distribution unto them, and unto all men <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Another cause of thanksgiving will be Gods moving your hearts towards them; they will see reason to bless God, who hath raised them up such friends in their great straits, so as they will both bless God on your behalf, for his Grace bestowed on you, that out of the Gentiles he hath picked out a people so subject to the Law of his Gospel; and also <ns0:hi>on their own behalf,</ns0:hi> that God hath stirred up a people to compassionate them in their deep distresses.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And by their prayer for you, which long af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter you for the exceeding grace of God in you <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Another way, by which the Glory of God will be promo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted, by your simple, free, and liberal Contribution, is, that by this he will have more Prayers, which also will redound to your advantage, for it will procure Prayers for you: and not Prayers only, but a great deal of <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ervent Love; so as they will long after your good, and after your acquaintance, when they shall receive such an experiment of the exceeding Grace of God in you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 Thanks <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> unto God for his unspeakable gift <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Interpreters are not agreed what the Apostle here mean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth by Gods <ns0:hi>unspeakable Gift.</ns0:hi> Some by it understand Christ, who is <ns0:hi>the Gift of God,</ns0:hi> and the Fountain of all Grace: and to this, the Epithet [<ns0:hi>unspeakable</ns0:hi>] doth best agree. Others un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstand the <ns0:hi>Gospel,</ns0:hi> by which the hearts of men are subdued, effectually disposed, and inclined to obey the Will of God. Others think it is to be understood of that habit of brotherly Love, which from the Spirit of Christ, by the Gospel, was wrought in the hearts of these <ns0:hi>Corinthians.</ns0:hi> If the last be meant, (to which the most incline) the Apostle declareth his firm perswasion of them, that they would obey him in this thing, and giveth God thanks for giving them such an heart. Seeing the Contribution was not yet made, though a year be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore they had declared their readiness to it, I should rather in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cline to interpret it concerning Christ; and that the Apostle concludeth this whole Discourse about contributing to the relief of these poor Members of Christ, with a general <ns0:hi>Doxology,</ns0:hi> or blessing of God for Jesus Christ, who is the Author and Fini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sher of all Grace, without such a particular reference to the pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceding Discourse; yet hereby hinting to them, that without the influence of his Grace they would, they could do nothing.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
